summary.text: Invertebrates are animals that neither develop nor retain a vertebral column, the spine or backbone.
The majority of animal species are invertebrates, and one estimate puts the figure at 97%.
The word is a convenience, since some so-called invertebrates, such as tunicates, are more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates.

facts.label: Size range
facts.value: From 10 micrometre myxozoans to 10 metre squid

facts.label: Word origin
facts.value: Latin vertebra, a joint, with in- meaning not

items.prompt: A tunicate has no backbone, yet it is more closely related to vertebrates than to other invertebrates. What does that show about the word invertebrate?

options.label: It names a true branch of animals that all share a recent ancestor
It groups animals by a missing trait, so it is a term of convenience rather than a true branch
It proves that tunicates were wrongly counted among animals
It shows that backbones evolved separately in every animal group

items.explain: Because some invertebrates are closer kin to vertebrates, the grouping is paraphyletic, and the term is one of convenience, not a taxon.

items.prompt: Grouping animals as winged or wingless puts insects, bats and birds together. What weakness does grouping animals by having no backbone share with that?

options.label: Both groupings leave out most of the animals alive today
Both groupings are too small to be of any practical use
Both groupings depend on size rather than on body features
The shared trait does not point to a clear common biological origin for the group

items.explain: The backbone distinction is one of convenience and is not based on any clear biologically homologous trait, much as having wings does not unite insects, bats and birds.

items.prompt: A garden worm has no bones and no hard shell, yet it holds its shape. What gives it a body structure?

options.label: A small internal bone running along its length
A hard outer shell like the ones beetles have
A fluid-filled body that works as a hydrostatic skeleton
A stiff spine that it grows in place of a backbone

items.explain: Many invertebrates, such as worms and jellyfish, have fluid-filled hydrostatic skeletons, while others have hard exoskeletons.

items.prompt: A male fiddler crab loses its oversized claw. What happens after he next moults?

options.label: He grows the large claw back on the same side
He grows a new large claw on the opposite side
He stays with one small claw for the rest of his life
He grows two large claws of equal size

items.explain: Fiddler crabs often have one claw much larger than the other, and a male that loses the large one grows another on the opposite side after moulting.

items.prompt: An invertebrate cannot live on sunlight and water alone. Why not?

options.label: Its lack of a backbone stops it from absorbing light
Only animals with a skeleton are able to digest food
As an animal, it is a heterotroph and must eat other organisms
It makes its own food but too slowly to live on

items.explain: Being animals, invertebrates are heterotrophs and need sustenance from consuming other organisms.

steps.text: Invertebrates are animals without a backbone.
Tunicates have no backbone, so they fit that description.
So tunicates must be more closely related to insects than to vertebrates.
So invertebrate marks one tidy branch of animal life.

paragraphs.heading: Animals without a backbone
paragraphs.text: Invertebrates are animals that never grow a backbone, also called a spine or vertebral column, and do not keep one either. The word comes from Latin: vertebra means a joint, and the prefix in- means "not" or "without". Most animal species are invertebrates, and one estimate puts the share at 97%. They range in size from myxozoans 10 μm across to the colossal squid, at 9–10 m long.

paragraphs.heading: Not a true family tree group
paragraphs.text: Biologists call the group paraphyletic: it takes in every animal except one branch, the vertebrates. Some animals counted as invertebrates, such as the tunicates and the Cephalochordata, are actually closer relatives of vertebrates than of other invertebrates. So the word does not name a real taxon the way Arthropoda or Vertebrata does. It is a term of convenience rather than a branch of the tree of life.

paragraphs.heading: Who belongs
paragraphs.text: Almost all invertebrates fall within one branch, the Protostomia, which holds arthropods, molluscs, annelids and flatworms. Other well-known ones are deuterostomes, such as echinoderms and tunicates, or sit outside that split altogether, such as cnidarians and sponges. Many invertebrate groups have more species, and more varied ones, than all the vertebrates put together. Of the invertebrate species that have been described, insects make up by far the largest number.

paragraphs.heading: Bodies without bone
paragraphs.text: In the older sense of the word, invertebrates have no skeleton of bone, either inside or outside the body. Their body plans differ enormously. Many, like jellyfish and worms, have a skeleton made of fluid, called a hydrostatic skeleton, while others, like insects and crustaceans, have a hard outer shell called an exoskeleton. As animals, they must eat other living things. With a few exceptions, such as the Porifera, their bodies are built of distinct tissues, usually with a digestive chamber that has one or two openings.

paragraphs.heading: Lopsided bodies
paragraphs.text: Most many-celled animals have some kind of symmetry, but a minority have none. All gastropods are asymmetric: snails and sea snails carry coiled shells, and even a slug, which looks even on the outside, has its breathing hole, the pneumostome, on its right side. Fiddler crabs and hermit crabs often have one claw much bigger than the other. If a male fiddler crab loses its big claw, it grows a new one on the opposite side after moulting.

paragraphs.heading: A handy label
paragraphs.text: Vertebrates make up such a small share of all animals that splitting the animal kingdom into vertebrates and invertebrates is of limited practical use. The only thing every invertebrate shares is the missing backbone. That is no more a real biological bond than wings are a reason to group insects, bats and birds together. Even so, the idea has lasted for more than a century, both in everyday speech and among zoologists, as a convenient name for animals that are not vertebrates.
